exercise1.prompt: colors = {"red", "green", "blue"}, add yellow, remove green, print the set

cases.name: blue, red and yellow are left

hiddenCases.name: add() and remove() change the set
hiddenCases.describe: add() to put yellow in and remove() to take green out

exercise1.hint: A set is built with curly braces and grows with add(), not append(). Sorting it is only a way to look at it here; a set itself keeps no order at all.

exercise2.prompt: set1 = {1, 2, 3, 4}, set2 = {3, 4, 5, 6}; print the intersection and the union
exercise2.hint: Three operators look alike and mean different things: & keeps what both have, | keeps everything, and - keeps what only the first one has. Say out loud which you want before picking the symbol.

questions.explain: The repeats never make it into the set, so only 1, 2 and 3 are stored. That is the property you use to strip duplicates out of a list.

questions.prompt: For a = {1, 2, 3} and b = {3, 4}, match each operator to its result.
questions.explain: & is the overlap, | is everything, and - is what the first set has to itself. `in` asks about one value and answers with a boolean.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true of a set?
choices: It stores each value at most once
It keeps the order you added things in
You can reach an item with an index
questions.explain: A set trades order and indexing for uniqueness and fast membership tests. If you need position, you wanted a list.

questions.prompt: colors.___("yellow") puts one new colour into a set.
questions.explain: append() belongs to lists. A set uses add(), and adding something it already holds changes nothing and raises nothing.
